title: ZTHR: A Pattern Language for Autonomous Software Delivery
excerpt: AI writes the code. The factory proves it. Two principles and thirty-three patterns for delivering software written by AI without making human code review the thing that holds quality together.
content_html:
Zero Trust – High Reliability

AI writes the code. The factory proves it.

ZTHR is a pattern language for software built by AI. Nothing is trusted because it says so, and quality comes from the environment the author works in, not from the author.

See it working: the Student Advocate

Map: how it fits together start here

Every part of the example on one page: the app, its admin, the evidence, the docs and the case.

The case write-up

What an AI factory can build, and what it is worth: business and technical.

About the app example

A reference app built entirely by agents under ZTHR fixtures: what it does and who it is for.

Use the app live

Sign in as any of twelve sample students, each a private copy for two hours.

App admin live

Catalog, moderation, scouts, admissions and outcome measures.

Evidence factory

Gates, walks, every test, mutation, the sensitive-data trace and the block library.

The full source GitHub

The app, the blocks, the gates, the pipeline and every journey card.

Discussion forum

Questions, experience reports and objections, in the open.

TL;DR

The whole idea in one paragraph

Generating code is now nearly free. Deciding whether it is right is not. So stop asking people to read every diff, and build a factory that cannot be fooled: governed parts that limit what can be built, checks proven to fail on the defects they exist to catch, and statements of user intent the author cannot rewrite. Let the models try as many times as it takes. Ship only what passes. Turn every miss into a new check.

Two principles

ASymmetric Zero Trust

No author, reviewer, model, operator or report gains authority by asserting success. A claim counts only on evidence the claimant does not control.

BThe Fixture Inversion

Quality moves out of the author's skill and into the environment. Generators iterate until the fixtures are satisfied.

The question every reviewer asks instead of "is this code good?"

Which fixture forces that, and has it been shown to bite?

Cite this work

Little, R. (2026). ZTHR: A Pattern Language for Autonomous Software Delivery (Version 1.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23826734
